title: Pattern: Real-Time Updates
summary: Push changes to clients with polling, SSE or WebSockets, route events between servers with pub/sub, and recover missed messages after reconnects.
body:
Chat, live sports scores, collaborative editors, ride tracking and notifications all need the server to tell clients about changes within about a second. HTTP request/response is client-initiated, so you need a delivery mechanism to the client and, once you have many servers, a way to route an event from whichever server produced it to whichever server holds the recipient's connection. Interviewers probe both halves: the client protocol and the server-side fan-out.

## Client delivery options

| Option | How it works | Latency | Good for | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Short polling | Client asks every N seconds | Up to N s | Low-frequency updates, simplest | Wasted requests; load scales with users × frequency |
| Long polling | Server holds the request until data arrives or ~30 s timeout | Near real time | Infrequent events, restrictive networks | One request per message; reconnect overhead |
| Server-Sent Events (SSE) | One long-lived HTTP response streaming events server → client | Near real time | Feeds, scores, notifications, LLM token streams | One-way; text only; client sends via normal HTTP |
| WebSocket | Upgraded TCP connection, full duplex | Lowest | Chat, games, collaborative editing | Stateful connections; load balancer and deploy complexity |
| WebRTC | Peer-to-peer media/data after signaling via your server | Lowest, P2P | Voice/video calls | Needs STUN/TURN for NAT traversal; complex; not for server fan-out |

Start with the simplest option that meets the latency requirement. SSE is underrated: it uses plain HTTP, the browser reconnects automatically, and it sends the `Last-Event-ID` header so the server can resume. Choose WebSockets when clients also send frequent messages over the same channel.

## Server-side fan-out

With one server, delivery is a local lookup. With 100 gateway servers each holding 50k connections, the sender and recipient are usually on different machines. Separate **connection gateways** (hold sockets, little logic) from **application services** (validate, persist, decide recipients), and connect them with pub/sub.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Sender"] --> G1["Gateway 1"]
    G1 --> S["Message service"]
    S --> DB[("Message store")]
    S --> PS[["Pub/sub: Redis or Kafka"]]
    PS --> G2["Gateway 2"]
    PS --> G3["Gateway 3"]
    G2 --> B["Recipient B"]
    G3 --> C["Recipient C"]
    REG[("Connection registry")] -.-> S
```

The sender's gateway forwards the message to the message service, which first persists it (assigning a per-conversation sequence number) and then publishes it. Gateways subscribed to the relevant channel push it down the open sockets of recipients B and C. The connection registry records which gateway currently holds each user, so the service can publish to that gateway's channel instead of broadcasting to all.

### Routing choices

- **Channel per user or room, gateways subscribe on demand.** When a user connects, its gateway subscribes to `user:{id}` (or `room:{id}`). Publishers do not need to know locations. Redis pub/sub handles this well up to a large number of channels, but it is fire-and-forget: a disconnected subscriber misses messages.
- **Connection registry.** Store `user_id → gateway_id` in Redis with a TTL refreshed by heartbeat; publish to `gateway:{id}`. Explicit, but the registry must be updated on every connect and disconnect.
- **Consistent hashing.** Route each user (or room) to a gateway by hashing its ID onto a ring, so any service can compute the owner without a lookup. When a gateway is added or removed, only about 1/N of users move and must reconnect. This requires a routing layer (for example the load balancer hashing on a user token) and works best when membership changes are rare.
- **Kafka** fits when you need durable, replayable streams (e.g. partition by conversation and let gateways or a delivery service consume), at the cost of higher latency and per-partition consumer limits.

### Fan-out on write vs on read

For one-to-many updates (feeds, followers), **fan-out on write** pushes to every follower's inbox or socket at send time: fast reads, expensive for accounts with millions of followers. **Fan-out on read** has each viewer pull from the sources they follow: cheap writes, slower reads. Use push for normal accounts and pull for celebrities.

## Presence, reconnects and catch-up

Real connections drop constantly: phones switch networks, laptops sleep, gateways redeploy.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as Gateway
    participant S as Message service
    C->>G: Connect, last_seq 41
    G->>S: Fetch conversation after 41
    S-->>G: Messages 42 to 45
    G-->>C: Replay 42 to 45
    G->>S: Subscribe live channel
    S-->>G: Message 46
    G-->>C: Push 46, client acks
```

On reconnect, the client reports the highest sequence number it has. The gateway fetches the gap from the durable store, replays it, then subscribes to the live channel. The client deduplicates by sequence number, which handles the overlap between replay and live delivery. The durable store is the source of truth; pub/sub is only the fast path.

- **Presence:** each connection heartbeats every ~30 s; the gateway writes `presence:{user}` with a ~60 s TTL. Expiry means offline. Publish presence changes lazily (only to users viewing that contact) because presence fan-out can exceed message traffic.
- **Reconnect storms:** when a gateway dies, its 50k clients reconnect at once. Use exponential backoff with jitter on clients and drain gateways gracefully on deploy (stop accepting, ask clients to reconnect over a few minutes).
- **Offline users:** persist first, then deliver via push notification; the client syncs on open.

## Failure modes and interview mistakes

- Treating Redis pub/sub as durable. It drops messages for disconnected subscribers; always persist and support catch-up.
- Choosing WebSockets by reflex for one-way updates where SSE or long polling would be simpler.
- Forgetting the load balancer: WebSockets need connection-aware balancing (least connections), long idle timeouts and graceful draining.
- Broadcasting every message to every gateway: cost grows as messages × gateways. Route by registry, channel or hash.
- No ordering story: use a per-conversation sequence assigned at the single writer, not client timestamps.
- Sizing ignored: 10M concurrent connections at ~50k per gateway means ~200 gateways, before headroom.

## How to use it in an interview

1. Pick the protocol from the requirement: direction of traffic, latency target, update frequency.
2. Size connections: concurrent users ÷ connections per gateway (tens of thousands is a reasonable assumption; memory per connection is the limit).
3. Draw gateways, a message service, a durable store and pub/sub; explain how an event reaches the right gateway.
4. Cover reconnect with sequence numbers, presence with TTL heartbeats, and fan-out strategy for large audiences.

Expect: "What happens when a gateway crashes?", "How do you guarantee ordering?", "How does a user on three devices get the message?" (subscribe all device connections to the same user channel and track a read cursor per device).

## Interview exercise

Design live score updates for a sports app: 5M concurrent viewers during a final, one score event every few seconds, plus a chat room per match with 200k active chatters. Choose a protocol for each feature, size the gateway fleet, and explain how a viewer who loses signal for 20 seconds catches up.

keyTakeaways: Pick the simplest client protocol that meets the latency and direction requirements; SSE covers many one-way cases.
Separate connection gateways from application logic and route events between them with pub/sub, a registry or consistent hashing.
Persist before publishing: pub/sub is the fast path, the durable store is the source of truth.
Clients reconnect with their last sequence number and fetch the gap, deduplicating by sequence.
Use TTL heartbeats for presence and jittered backoff to survive reconnect storms.
